title.title: Kaplansky's zero-divisor conjecture fails
title.subtitle: Claim: a torsion-free group $G$ and nonzero $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{F}_2[G]$ with $\alpha\beta = 0$

plain: In this group's arithmetic, two nonzero things can multiply to zero, which was thought impossible

panels.caption: schematic: equal colours are equal group elements, so they cancel mod 2

lines.tex: G \text{ torsion-free, finitely presented, finite 2-dim } K(G,1)

beats.text: Multiply $\alpha = \sum g_i$ by $\beta = \sum h_j$: every product term, schematically
The construction makes every coefficient of $\alpha\beta$ an even count of products
Over $\mathbb{F}_2$ they all cancel: a zero divisor in a torsion-free group algebra

steps: Build a group from two finite graphs drawn in a rose
Multiply: every group element appears an even number of times

achievement.label: Kaplansky's zero-divisor conjecture (1950s)
statement: G \text{ torsion-free} \;\Longrightarrow\; K[G] \text{ has no zero divisors}
achievement.context: Before: true for orderable, unique-product, elementary amenable groups; the unit conjecture fell in 2021
achievement.note: Over $\mathbb{F}_2$ only; characteristic zero is untouched

verify.detail: The Comparator statement includes torsion-free, finitely presented, finite 2-dim $K(G,1)$ and $\alpha\beta = 0$
verify.ourCheck: We read the Comparator statement; we did not run the checker

voice.text: Kaplansky asked if a torsion-free group algebra can have zero divisors; most expected not.
In the product, every group element appears an even number of times: it cancels.
Claimed: two nonzero elements whose product is zero.

sources.quote: Kaplansky asked in the 1950s whether the group algebra $K[G]$ of a torsion-free group over a field can have zero divisors.
Giles Gardam disproved the neighbouring unit conjecture in 2021
arranges that every coefficient of $\alpha\beta$ comes from an even number of products
This is over $\mathbb F_2$ only. Characteristic zero, where the conjecture connects to the Atiyah conjecture, is untouched.
Standard axioms; review 'unchecked'; I did not run the checker.
